extracted.intended_audience: DOE Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) communications staff, web coordinators, and authors of DOE/CMEI web and outreach content (press releases, webpages, reports)
extracted.subtask_description: Style and usage rules for writing DOE CMEI web pages, news items, reports, captions, figures, and other outreach content. Covers grammar, punctuation, capitalization, citations, units, trademarks, accessibility/formatting, and web-specific guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: a, an
rubrics_metrics.description: Use "a" before any acronym or word that begins with a consonant sound. Use "an" before any acronym or word that begins with a vowel sound. An acronym is pronounced as a word (e.g., a HEPA filter); an initialism is pronounced as its letters (e.g., an NGO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a light-water reactor; an LWR; a request for proposals; an RFP; a NASA astronaut; a Project Management Plan; an PMP.

rubrics_metrics.name: abbreviations, acronyms, and initialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out the full name on first use, followed immediately by the abbreviation/acronym/initialism in parentheses. Avoid abbreviations unless the phrase appears more than once or the abbreviation is better recognized than the full name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a glossary if publication is ≥50 pages and contains ≥20 acronyms. Avoid using in headlines or page headers unless well recognized. Exception: acronyms/initialisms may be used for CMEI News and GovDelivery blog items. Use a shortened name on second reference. Common items that don't require spelling are listed (e.g., no., vs., ASAP, R&D).

rubrics_metrics.name: technical measurement units
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out a technical abbreviation in full in text when used without numerals. Abbreviate units of measurement when used with a numeral; use a space between numeral and unit except for a few exceptions (% , ° , $, < , ¢).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In text without numeral: “a few centimeters” not “a few cm.” With numeral: 15 cm; 15 m; 15 dB; 15% ; $15; <15 W. For units pluralization omit the s (15 cm not 15 cms).

rubrics_metrics.name: pluralization of abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small s (no apostrophe) for plurals of most abbreviations. For plurals of units of measurement, omit the s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PUCs not PUC’s; CFCs not CFC’s; 15 cm not 15 cms; 6 m not 6 ms; 75 dB not 75 dBs; 40 W not 40 Ws.

rubrics_metrics.name: possessiveness with names and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a possessive is used with a name or term, place the apostrophe after both the spelled-out name/term and the acronym/abbreviation; preference is to rewrite to avoid the possessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE's) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) is in charge of the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: abbreviating equations and references
rubrics_metrics.description: You can abbreviate “equation” and “reference” when used with numbers. Spell them out at the beginning of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Eq. 1-1, Eq. 2-7, and Ref. 10. Use "Equation 2-1" when starting a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract usually accompanies a journal article or conference paper and is an important indexing and research tool; it typically runs 200–250 words and summarizes purpose, scope, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract may include a brief description of methods used to reach conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid use of academic degrees unless necessary to establish credentials. When written out, do not use an acronym unless used multiple times on a page or as part of a person's title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periods between letters (Ph.D., B.A., M.A., LL.D.) except MBA. Academic title 'Dr.' only for medical degrees; do not capitalize level of degree or subject when written out; use an apostrophe in bachelor's, master’s degree, etc. Place degree acronyms after a name, set off with commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: acknowledgments in reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge reviews, funding, and assistance in CMEI technical reports and papers; acknowledgments can go in a preface, foreword, or a separate page and often follow the main text in journal articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals usually have instructions for authors on acknowledgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: addresses and state abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use U.S. Postal Service two-letter abbreviations for states in bibliographies, references, and full addresses; in running text, spell out state names (except D.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.O. Box 123; Denver, CO 80101. In text: The state energy office is stepping up solar retrofit activities in Massachusetts.

rubrics_metrics.name: air conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two words when used as a noun and hyphenate when used as an adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Air conditioning is energy intensive. The efficiency of the air-conditioning system can be improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Recovery and Reinvestment Act naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out the full name on first reference and use 'Recovery Act' on subsequent references instead of 'ARRA'; do not put 'Recovery Act' in parentheses after the full name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct example: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 was designed to spur economic growth ... Through the Recovery Act, DOE provided billions ... Incorrect: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (ARRA).

rubrics_metrics.name: ampersand usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ampersands (&) with acronyms and initialisms (e.g., R&D), left/right navigation menus, and website top banners and in official company or initiative names; do not use & to mean 'and' otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: PG&E; Leadership in Energy & Environmental Design; R&D. Incorrect: Research & Development (in running copy).

rubrics_metrics.name: appendices formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Include detailed background or technical information in appendices; large tables belong in an appendix. If more than one appendix, title with letters; if only one, title it 'Appendix.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label figures/tables to correspond with appendix letter (Figure A-1, Table B-2). Even with one appendix, label tables/figures with letters (Figure A-1).

rubrics_metrics.name: assure / ensure / insure
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish meanings: 'assure' means to give confidence; 'ensure' means to make certain; 'insure' means to obtain insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The manufacturer assured the group ... Ensure the lid is fitted properly ... The laboratory must insure the new equipment ...

rubrics_metrics.name: author-date citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred citation style for CMEI reports and papers is author-date; do not use a comma between the author's last name and the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (Holdren 2001; Kalicki and Goldwyn 2005). See references and citations section for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: bulleted lists: minimum and parallel construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A bulleted list requires at least two items. Make items parallel in construction (same part of speech), and ensure they are either all phrases or all complete sentences. Punctuate items consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin each item with a capital letter and end with a period or terminal punctuation unless the bullets are short noun phrases or single words (then omit end punctuation except on final bullet). Do not use commas or semicolons at the end of bullets. Use numbered/lettered lists if you will refer to items elsewhere. Formatting: first level indented 0.25 in., text begins at 0.5 in.; subsequent levels indented 0.5 in.; in multi-line items follow each with 6-pt space. Web CSS governs website bullets; include spacing between text above bullets and first bullet; consider space between long bulleted items.

rubrics_metrics.name: capitalization: proper names and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper names (government programs, projects, formal groups, companies, titles before a name, specific geographic areas, ethnic groups). Capitalize main words of table titles and most headings/subheadings; lowercase articles and short conjunctions unless they begin the heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sandia National Laboratories; President and Chief Executive Officer Christine Johnson; PV Program Five-Year Plan. Capitalize verbs including 'is' and 'are' and the word 'to' in infinitives in headings. For figure captions, capitalize only the first word and proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: taxonomic names and italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize taxonomic divisions higher than species and put genera, species, and varieties in italics. Spell out at first mention then abbreviate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clostridium thermocellum (first mention) then C. thermocellum (subsequent); Escherichia coli then E. coli.

rubrics_metrics.name: captions for photos and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Accompany substantive photos, figures, and images with captions. Begin captions with a capitalized word and use lowercase thereafter (except proper nouns and abbreviations). Do not include a period at the end unless it’s a complete sentence or there's a subcaption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete sentence with a verb is preferred. If crediting a photographer, italicize the credit and omit a period. Example: Photo by Randy Montoya, Sandia Labs. Follow CMEI Communications Standards for placement/formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: chemical terms hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a hyphen in most chemical expressions, even when used as modifiers; use hyphens after prefixes when standard for certain chemical formulas and for mixtures/combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No hyphen: carbon dioxide levels, hydrogen ion activity. Standard: L(+)-2,3-butanediol, trans-glycol. Mixtures: hexane-benzene.

rubrics_metrics.name: colons usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use colons to introduce numbered/bulleted lists, series, questions, or amplifications and to separate parts of a ratio. Capitalize the first word after a colon only if it's a proper noun or the start of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a colon after a verb or preposition that introduces a list (are, includes, to, with, between). Don’t use colon where a comma is appropriate. Example: We test three types of collectors: flat plates, evacuated tubes, and parabolic troughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: commas and serial comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate items in a series, including the serial (Oxford) comma; CMEI prefers Chicago Style on this issue. Use commas to separate parts of compound sentences when each part has its own subject and verb and to set off nonessential phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: We develop solar thermal, wind, biomass, and photovoltaic energy technologies. Use commas to enclose state names after cities and years after month and day. Do not use commas to separate compound subjects or compound verbs. See 'which and that' for restrictive vs nonrestrictive usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: compound modifiers and hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a hyphen to indicate compound modifiers that create a single meaning; verb phrases with adverbs often are two words, while noun/adjective forms may be one word or hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flat-plate collector; low-level radiation; last-minute addition; five-year plan; fatigure-induced wear. Use hyphens to prevent ambiguity: 'defect-causing gas' vs 'defect causing gas'. Prefixes generally don't need hyphens unless the following word is a proper noun or capitalized (pre-Civil War) or prefixes 'ex-', 'self-', 'quasi-'.

rubrics_metrics.name: dates formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use month, numeral, and year (American order) for announcements and deadlines. Abbreviate months only when used with a specific date for Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.; spell out months when used alone or with a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sept. 20, 2021; Jan. 1–5, 2019. Do not use ordinal numbers (1st) unless in prepared remarks/speeches. Date ranges use en dash with no spaces. Decades do not include apostrophes unless preceded by 'the'. When a phrase lists only month and year, do not separate year with commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: degree symbol and temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the degree symbol (º) next to the temperature scale symbol with no space. Use K for kelvins (no degree symbol) and leave a space before K. Repeat degree symbol in ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 36ºC; 85ºF; 32º–36ºC; 85 K.

rubrics_metrics.name: disclaimer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE requires that CMEI publications include a disclaimer; the specific disclaimer depends on the type of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See CMEI-Branded Publications Developed by Third Parties for applicable disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: dollars and large numbers formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Express thousands with commas. Express millions/billions/trillions using numerals and the words million/billion/trillion; abbreviations M or B acceptable in headlines. In technical reports, use $ for costs < $1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $5,000; $3 million budget; $1.2 billion; $0.25; Use no hyphens even when phrase used as adjective (a $4.2 trillion budget).

rubrics_metrics.name: e.g. and i.e. punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both abbreviations are always followed by a comma and are preceded by a semicolon when a clause (with subject and verb) follows them; do not italicize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a semicolon before 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' and a comma after when a clause follows. Example: Bring any two items; e.g., sleeping bags and tents are in short supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: ellipses in quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ellipsis marks (three periods with spaces or the ellipsis symbol) to indicate omission. If words preceding an ellipsis form a grammatically correct sentence, put a period then the ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually, ellipses aren’t needed at the beginning or end of quotes, just within them. To add words, enclose additions in brackets. To indicate omitted whole paragraphs, center three asterisks (* * *) between paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: email (e- terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable to use 'email' (no hyphen) for 'electronic mail'. Use a hyphen with other e- terms like e-book, e-business, e-commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: I sent an email to everyone involved with the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: ENERGY STAR trademark usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Always show ENERGY STAR in all capitals; include the registration mark (®) on first use except in headlines or headers (then include ® in first use in body); after first use do not repeat ®.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline: What Is ENERGY STAR? Body: ENERGY STAR® is the government-backed symbol ...

rubrics_metrics.name: sources for figures and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the sources of all figures and tables originally published by others; if copyrighted, permission may be needed. Add the source at the end of a figure caption or note following a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Source: Hansen, W.L.; Pearton, S.J.; Haller, E.E. (1984). Appl. Phys. Lett. 44:606.

rubrics_metrics.name: spaces after sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only one space after a colon and between sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: Use only one space between one sentence and the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: semicolons usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semicolons to connect closely related independent clauses or before conjunctive adverbs linking two clauses; use semicolons in complex lists where items contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolon before conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, thus, etc.) and place a comma after the adverb. Example: We used the Schartz-Metterklume method; however, the problems ... Use semicolons to separate items in a series when items contain commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: SI (metric) system preference
rubrics_metrics.description: CMEI follows national and society policies by using the SI (International System of Units) to express technical measurements. English units may follow metric ones or be used alone in special cases by audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: He vowed to walk 62 miles (100 kilometers) in a week. Prefer metric first with English equivalents in parentheses when appropriate. See NIST guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: slash (solidus) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a slash for fractions and to express quotient or junctions/interfaces; with abbreviated units slash stands for 'per' but spell out 'per' when units are spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gas/liquid interface; 2 g/cm2; several cubic meters per second; a few cents per kilowatt-hour. In print break long URLs at a slash where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: smart grid lowercase
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowercase 'smart grid' unless it begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A video on the smart grid explains its impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: states and countries usage and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In running text, consistently spell out state names rather than using postal abbreviations; use a comma between city and state and also after a state or country name (unless ending sentence). Do not abbreviate country names when used as nouns; use U.S. as adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use postal abbreviations in addresses/reference lists. Examples: He was traveling from Nashville, Tennessee, to Austin, Texas. The United States; U.S. DOE program. Always lowercase 'country'/'countries' as common noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: statistical terms hyphenation and case
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to statistical or graphical terms, use a hyphen but no italics and do not use capital letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: p-value; t-test; y-axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: that and which (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'which' for nonrestrictive (nonessential) phrases and clauses and 'that' for restrictive (essential) phrases and clauses; nonrestrictive clauses are set off with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which: The paper, which she has been working on for three weeks, discusses string theory. That: The paper that he completed recently will be presented in New York.

rubrics_metrics.name: who and whom
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'who' as subject (references to humans/animals with names). Use 'whom' when someone is the object of a verb or preposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The woman who rented the room left the window open. Whom do you wish to see?

rubrics_metrics.name: URL and hyperlink best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: On websites, embed URLs in text and prefer the word 'website' over 'URL' in copy. In print, do not embed URLs; break long URLs at slashes if they extend beyond one line. When embedding hyperlinks, keep the hyperlink as short as possible (ideally three words or fewer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include https:// prefix on most URLs in print unless necessary — test before removing. Shorten URLs (remove /index.html) while ensuring functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: trademark symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trademark symbols with DOE-owned/registered programs/products on first mention; omit the symbol thereafter. Do not use trademark symbols with third-party products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of common government-owned trademarks provided (BUILD4SCALE™, Energy Earthshots™, ENERGY STAR®, etc.). No space before the symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribe/Tribal Nation capitalization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend capitalizing 'Tribe,' 'Tribal,' 'Native,' 'Nation,' 'Tribal Leader,' 'Tribal Council,' and 'Alaska Native Village' as a matter of respect in all cases when referring to Native American Tribes; 'Tribal' capitalized as proper noun or generic modifier but not in unrelated tribal references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize when referring to Tribal entities and programs. Do not capitalize when referring generically to tribal lines across the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: units of measurement and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals with units of measurement and time in technical papers and reports, even when the number is less than 10. Leave a space between numeral and unit except with $, °, and %; in outreach content spell out numbers less than 10 when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State metric units first with English equivalents in parentheses unless industry standard dictates otherwise. Examples: 2 kW; 16.8%; 3 m; 8-hour days; $2 billion; 45°; 38.1 m (125 ft).

rubrics_metrics.name: zero before decimal
rubrics_metrics.description: For numbers less than one, place a zero before the decimal.
